title: How do you handle a hot row that many requests update at once (e.g. a shared like/stock counter) — counter sharding (split into N sub-counters and sum) or buffering increments in Redis and periodically syncing to the DB?
shortTitle: How do you handle a hot row that many requests update at once

s1_definition.profdef: A hot row is a single database row that many concurrent requests try to update at the same time, such as a shared counter, creating lock contention that serializes all writers and throttles throughput. The two main remedies are counter sharding, where you split the single logical counter into N physical sub-counter rows so writers spread across them and the true value is their sum, and in-memory buffering, where you accumulate increments in a fast store like Redis and periodically flush the aggregate to the database, turning many small row updates into few batched ones.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a single donation box at National Bank of India where thousands of customers must drop coins one at a time, so everyone queues and it is painfully slow because only one hand fits in the slot. Counter sharding puts out twenty donation boxes so twenty people donate at once, and at the end you add up all twenty boxes for the total. Buffering instead lets a fast assistant collect everyone's coins in a bucket and tip the whole bucket into the main box once a minute, so the heavy main box is touched rarely.
s1_definition.oneliner: A hot row serializes writers on one lock, so you either shard the counter into N sub-rows that writers spread across and sum on read, or buffer increments in Redis and flush the aggregate to the database periodically.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A hot row is a single database row that many concurrent requests try to update at the same time, such as a shared counter, creating lock contention that serializes all writers and throttles throughput. The two main remedies are counter sharding, where you split the single logical counter into N physical sub-counter rows so writers spread across them and the true value is their sum, and in-memory buffering, where you accumulate increments in a fast store like Redis and periodically flush the aggregate to the database, turning many small row updates into few batched ones.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a single donation box at National Bank of India where thousands of customers must drop coins one at a time, so everyone queues and it is painfully slow because only one hand fits in the slot. Counter sharding puts out twenty donation boxes so twenty people donate at once, and at the end you add up all twenty boxes for the total. Buffering instead lets a fast assistant collect everyone's coins in a bucket and tip the whole bucket into the main box once a minute, so the heavy main box is touched rarely.

**One line to remember:** A hot row serializes writers on one lock, so you either shard the counter into N sub-rows that writers spread across and sum on read, or buffer increments in Redis and flush the aggregate to the database periodically.

sections.s2_technical:
First understand why a hot row hurts. Every update to a row takes a row-level lock for the duration of the transaction. If one row, say the like count on a viral post or the stock count of a popular item, receives thousands of concurrent increments, those transactions queue on that single lock and effectively run one after another. The database is not short of CPU; it is serialized on one lock, so throughput collapses and latency spikes even though the rest of the system is idle. The goal of both remedies is to reduce contention on any single lock.

Counter sharding splits the one logical counter into N physical sub-counter rows, often keyed by something like `counter_id` plus a shard index from 0 to N minus 1. A writer picks a shard, typically at random or by hashing the request, and increments only that shard's row, so the write load spreads across N locks instead of one and contention drops by roughly a factor of N. The true value is obtained on read by summing all shards, `SELECT SUM(value) FROM counter_shards WHERE counter_id = ?`. For example with sixteen shards, sixteen writers can proceed in parallel, each on its own row. The trade-off is that reads become a sum over N rows, so you choose N to balance write contention against read cost, and you accept that a point-in-time read is only eventually consistent with in-flight writes. Sharding keeps the data in the database and is the right choice when you need durability on every increment and strong-ish counting with just less contention.

Buffering increments in a fast store trades immediacy for throughput. Instead of hitting the database on every increment, you increment an in-memory counter in Redis with its atomic `INCR`, which handles enormous rates on a single key because it is single-threaded and in-memory, and a background job periodically reads the accumulated delta and applies it to the database in one batched update, `UPDATE counter SET value = value + ? WHERE id = ?`. This collapses, say, ten thousand increments per second into one database write per flush interval, nearly eliminating database contention. The trade-offs are that the database is now stale between flushes, so reads should come from Redis for freshness, and that a Redis failure between flushes risks losing the un-flushed delta unless Redis is persistent or you flush frequently, so this suits counters where small, rare loss or brief staleness is acceptable, like social like counts, more than strict financial balances.

Choosing between them, and senior nuances: sharding when every increment must be durable and you want the source of truth to stay in the database, buffering when you need extreme write throughput and can tolerate staleness and small loss. They also compose, for example sharded Redis counters flushed to the database. For true financial correctness, like a real account balance, you usually avoid a hot shared counter entirely by modeling increments as individual append-only ledger entries and computing the balance as a sum or a maintained aggregate, which removes the single hot row by design. Other complementary techniques include using the database's atomic increment to keep each transaction tiny so the lock is held briefly, batching increments at the application layer before writing, and for the last-unit stock case combining a buffered counter with a reconciliation and a hard stock guard so you never oversell. The principle throughout is to spread or batch the contention rather than fighting one lock.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A National Bank of India promotional post tracking "number of customers who opened a fixed deposit today" used one counter row, and during a campaign thousands of concurrent increments queued on that row's lock and the API slowed to a crawl. This is exactly the hot-row problem, addressed by sharding the counter across many rows.

Problem 2 — A "likes" counter on a banking community post needed extreme write throughput but only approximate freshness. This is exactly the buffering case, accumulating increments in Redis and flushing to the database periodically.

Problem 3 — The team briefly used a hot counter for an actual account balance and hit both contention and correctness worries. This is exactly why a true balance should be an append-only ledger summed or aggregated, not a hot shared counter.

Our mini-project demonstrates both remedies. The code defines a `ShardedCounter` that spreads increments across N rows and sums on read, a `BufferedCounter` that increments in an in-memory Redis-like store and flushes to a database periodically, and a demo that fires many concurrent increments at each, showing the correct total with far less contention than a single hot row.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: ten thousand concurrent increments fired at the sharded counter and at the buffered counter.

Step 1: For the sharded counter, each of the ten thousand increments picks a random shard from the sixteen available and increments only that shard. Because writers spread across sixteen rows, up to sixteen can proceed in parallel instead of all queuing on one lock, so contention drops roughly sixteenfold.

Step 2: When the total is read, the counter sums all sixteen shards, producing exactly ten thousand. The logical value is correct; it was simply stored across many physical rows to spread the write load.

Step 3: For the buffered counter, each increment does a fast in-memory increment of the Redis-like buffer, which can absorb an enormous rate on a single key because it is in-memory and atomic. The database is not touched per increment.

Step 4: The background flusher periodically takes the accumulated delta from the buffer, resetting it atomically, and applies it to the database in one batched update. So ten thousand increments become only a handful of database writes, nearly eliminating database contention.

Step 5: After a final flush the database value equals ten thousand. The counter was correct, but the heavy database row was written rarely instead of ten thousand times, at the cost of brief staleness between flushes.

```
2026-10-24 14:28:10 INFO    SHARDED total = 10000 (expected 10000)
2026-10-24 14:28:10 INFO    FLUSH +4210 to DB for post_likes → 4210
2026-10-24 14:28:10 INFO    FLUSH +5790 to DB for post_likes → 10000
2026-10-24 14:28:10 INFO    BUFFERED db value = 10000 (expected 10000)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── The PROBLEM: one hot row ──
  10,000 writers ─┐
                  ▼
           [ counter row ]  ← ONE lock → all writers serialize → slow

  ── Remedy 1: counter sharding ──
  10,000 writers → pick random shard 0..15
    │   ├─ shard0  ++   ┐
    │   ├─ shard1  ++   │ 16 rows, 16 locks → ~16x less contention
    │   ├─ ...          │
    │   └─ shard15 ++   ┘
    ▼
  READ: SUM(shard0..shard15) = 10,000  (eventually consistent point-in-time)

  ── Remedy 2: buffering + periodic flush ──
  10,000 writers → Redis INCR key (in-memory, atomic, huge rate)
    │  buffer accumulates deltas
    ▼ every 200ms
  flusher: delta = GETSET(key,0) → UPDATE db SET v=v+delta (ONE batched write)
    │
    ▼
  DB value = 10,000  (reads served from Redis for freshness; DB stale between flushes)
```

```
  ── Class Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ ShardedCounter   │          │ BufferedCounter       │
  │ - shards[N]      │          │ - redisBuffer (INCR)  │
  │ + increment()    │          │ - dbValue             │
  │ + total()=SUM    │          │ + increment()         │
  └──────────────────┘          │ + flushNow()/flusher  │
  ┌──────────────────┐          └──────────────────────┘
  │ HotCounter (bad) │ one lock → contention
  └──────────────────┘

  ── Decision Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────
  Every increment must be durable, truth in DB? → counter sharding
  Need extreme throughput, tolerate staleness/small loss? → buffering
  Real money balance? → append-only ledger aggregate (avoid hot row)

  ── Call Chain (buffered) ─────────────────────────────────────
  1. increment() ×10,000 → redisBuffer.incr (in-memory)
  2. flusher: delta = getAndSet(0)
  3. dbValue += delta  (one batched UPDATE)
  4. read → Redis (fresh) ; DB catches up each flush
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
I start by explaining why a hot row is slow, because the remedies only make sense once you see the cause. Every update to a row takes a row-level lock for the duration of its transaction, so when one row, like a viral post's like count or a popular item's stock, receives thousands of concurrent increments, those transactions queue on that single lock and effectively run one at a time. The database is not short of CPU; it is serialized on one lock, so throughput collapses and latency spikes while the rest of the system sits idle. Both remedies exist to reduce contention on any single lock.

Counter sharding splits the one logical counter into N physical sub-counter rows. A writer picks a shard, usually at random or by hashing, and increments only that shard, so the write load spreads across N locks instead of one and contention drops by roughly a factor of N, and the true value is obtained on read by summing all the shards. The trade-off is that reads become a sum over N rows and a point-in-time read is only eventually consistent with in-flight writes, so I choose N to balance write contention against read cost. Sharding keeps every increment durable in the database, so I reach for it when the source of truth must stay in the database and I just need less contention.

Buffering trades immediacy for raw throughput. Instead of touching the database per increment, I increment an in-memory counter in Redis with its atomic INCR, which absorbs a huge rate on a single key because it is in-memory and single-threaded, and a background job periodically takes the accumulated delta and applies it to the database in one batched update. That collapses ten thousand increments into a handful of database writes and nearly eliminates contention. The trade-offs are that the database is stale between flushes, so I serve reads from Redis for freshness, and that a Redis failure between flushes can lose the un-flushed delta unless Redis is persistent or I flush often, so buffering suits approximate counters like social likes far more than strict balances. The two also compose, such as sharded Redis counters flushed to the database.

On my project at National Bank of India a campaign counter of fixed deposits opened today was a single hot row that throttled the API under load, and I sharded it across sixteen rows so writers spread out and the total came from a sum. A community-post like counter needed extreme throughput with only approximate freshness, so I buffered increments in Redis and flushed periodically. The most important lesson I learned, and the nuance I always add, is that for real money I do not use a hot shared counter at all: a true account balance is modeled as append-only ledger entries and computed as a sum or a maintained aggregate, which removes the single hot row by design and keeps the correctness guarantees that sharding and buffering deliberately relax.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that a hot row serializes all writers on one lock, so I either shard the counter into N sub-rows that writers spread across and sum on read when every increment must stay durable in the database, or buffer increments in Redis and flush the aggregate to the database periodically when I need extreme throughput and can tolerate staleness, and for real money I avoid the hot row entirely with an append-only ledger aggregate.

keyPoints: Horizontal scaling: add more instances behind load balancer
Vertical scaling: bigger machine — has limits
Auto-scaling: based on CPU, memory, request rate metrics
Sharding: partition data across databases for write scalability
